questions.stem: What is the difference between a contaminant and a pollutant?
options: A contaminant harms living things; a pollutant is present but causes no harm
A contaminant is present above natural levels; a pollutant is one that causes harm
A contaminant is always a solid; a pollutant is always a gas or a dissolved liquid
A contaminant comes from nature; a pollutant is any substance released by people
questions.explanation: A contaminant is a substance present where it would not normally be, or above background levels. It becomes a pollutant when it has, or is likely to have, harmful effects on organisms or the environment.

questions.stem: Tests show a trace of a pesticide in a river, at a concentration far below any level known to affect aquatic life. How is the pesticide best described?
options: As a contaminant, because it is present but not causing harm
As a pollutant, because any human-made chemical is a pollutant
As a nutrient, because it is dissolved in the river water
As a pollutant, because it came from a diffuse source
questions.explanation: The pesticide is present above natural levels, which makes it a contaminant, but there is no evidence of harm, so it is not yet a pollutant. Being human-made or coming from a diffuse source does not by itself make a substance a pollutant.

questions.stem: A biodegradable pollutant is one that:
options: is released from many scattered sources across a catchment
can be broken down into simpler substances by decomposers
builds up in the fatty tissue of animals over their lifetime
dissolves in water and spreads evenly through a waterway
questions.explanation: Biodegradable substances, such as food waste and sewage, are broken down by bacteria and fungi. Accumulation in fatty tissue describes persistent, fat-soluble pollutants.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties makes a pollutant most likely to cause long-term harm far from where it was released?
options: Persistent and mobile in air or water
Biodegradable and soluble in water
Biodegradable and released at one point
Non-persistent and quickly diluted
questions.explanation: A persistent pollutant does not break down for a long time, and if it is also carried by air or water it can travel and build up far from its source. Biodegradable and non-persistent substances break down before travelling far.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a point source of pollution?
options: Exhaust from vehicles on a city's road network
Sediment eroding from many forestry roads
A discharge pipe from a fish processing factory
Fertiliser washing off farms across a catchment
questions.explanation: A point source releases pollution from a single identifiable location, such as a pipe or chimney. Farm runoff, traffic exhaust and road erosion come from many scattered sources, so they are diffuse.

questions.stem: Why is diffuse source pollution usually harder to control than point source pollution?
options: It is always more toxic, so it cannot be treated by any known technology at all
It only occurs at night, so it is very difficult for regulators to measure it
It enters the ocean directly, so it never passes through any river or estuary
It comes from many scattered sources, so no single outlet can be treated
questions.explanation: A point source can be monitored, licensed and treated at the outlet, but diffuse pollution arrives from many places across a landscape. Controlling it needs changes in land management by many people rather than one treatment plant.

questions.stem: Bioaccumulation is the:
options: breakdown of a pollutant by bacteria in soil, sediment or water
growth of algae in water enriched by nitrogen and phosphorus
build-up of a substance in one organism's tissues over its lifetime
increase in a substance's concentration at each higher trophic level
questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation occurs within a single organism when a substance is taken in faster than it is broken down or excreted. The increase from one trophic level to the next is biomagnification.

questions.stem: Mercury levels in a lake are measured as: water 0.00002 ppm, zooplankton 0.002 ppm, small fish 0.04 ppm, predatory fish 0.4 ppm. By what factor did the concentration increase from small fish to predatory fish?
options: 10 times
20 times
100 times
200 times
questions.explanation: 0.4 / 0.04 = 10. The increase from zooplankton to small fish is 20 times, and from water to zooplankton is 100 times, which are tempting if the wrong pair of levels is used.

questions.stem: Which combination of properties allows a substance to biomagnify along a food chain?
options: Persistent, fat-soluble and not readily excreted
Biodegradable, water-soluble and easily excreted
Persistent, water-soluble and readily excreted
Biodegradable, fat-soluble and quickly broken down
questions.explanation: A substance that is not broken down and is stored in fat stays in the body, so each predator receives the accumulated load of the many prey it eats. Water-soluble substances are usually excreted in urine and do not build up.

questions.stem: Black bream, a predatory fish in a Tasmanian estuary with heavy metals in its sediments, have been found to carry higher mercury levels than many other species. Which is the best explanation?
options: Bream feed on plants only, and aquatic plants make mercury by photosynthesis
Mercury biomagnifies, so long-lived predators accumulate it from the prey they eat
Bream absorb mercury mainly through their gills, so it never passes along food chains
Mercury breaks down quickly in prey, so only predators are exposed to its toxic form
questions.explanation: Methylmercury is persistent and stored in tissues, so it increases at each trophic level and builds up in long-lived predators. Bream eat invertebrates and small fish, not only plants, and plants do not produce mercury.

questions.stem: Persistent organochlorine insecticides such as DDT have been detected in seals and seabirds living far from farmland. Which process best explains this?
options: The animals made the chemicals in their own bodies as part of normal metabolism
The chemicals were sprayed directly on the animals' feeding grounds at sea
The chemicals broke down in the ocean into new substances that are harmless
The chemicals travelled in water and air, then biomagnified up marine food chains
questions.explanation: Persistent chemicals are carried by rivers, ocean currents and the atmosphere, and because they do not break down they become concentrated in top predators. Animals do not make insecticides, and harmless breakdown products would not be detected as the original chemicals.

questions.stem: Eutrophication is caused mainly by excess inputs of:
options: calcium and magnesium
sodium and chloride
nitrogen and phosphorus
carbon dioxide and oxygen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and phosphorus are the nutrients that usually limit plant and algal growth in waterways, so adding them triggers algal blooms. Sodium and chloride raise salinity rather than causing blooms.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes eutrophication in a lake?
options: Nutrients enter, algae bloom, algae die, decomposers use oxygen, fish die
Algae bloom, nutrients enter, fish die, decomposers add oxygen, algae die
Fish die, nutrients enter, algae die, oxygen rises, decomposers bloom
Nutrients enter, oxygen rises, algae die, decomposers bloom, fish thrive
questions.explanation: Extra nutrients fuel an algal bloom; when the algae die, aerobic decomposers use up dissolved oxygen, and fish and invertebrates suffocate. Decomposition removes oxygen rather than adding it.

questions.stem: Biological oxygen demand (BOD) is a measure of:
options: the oxygen that dissolves into water from the air at the surface
the oxygen used by microorganisms to break down organic matter in water
the oxygen produced by aquatic plants and algae through photosynthesis
the oxygen that fish need per kilogram of body mass to survive
questions.explanation: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen that microbes consume while decomposing organic material, usually measured over five days. A high BOD means a lot of organic matter is present and oxygen is likely to be depleted.

questions.stem: A creek downstream of a food factory has a much higher BOD than a site upstream. What is the most likely consequence for the creek downstream?
options: Dissolved oxygen falls, which can kill fish and sensitive insects
Dissolved oxygen rises, which allows more fish to live in the creek
The water becomes saltier, which kills freshwater plants on the banks
The water becomes clearer, which lets more light reach the creek bed
questions.explanation: High BOD means microbes are using a lot of oxygen to decompose organic waste, lowering dissolved oxygen. Fish and invertebrates that need well-oxygenated water die or move away.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the BOD of a river?
options: A spill of milk and dairy effluent from a factory
Replanting native trees along the river's banks
Removal of organic sludge from the river bed
Installation of a sediment trap on a stormwater drain
questions.explanation: Milk and dairy effluent are rich in organic matter that bacteria decompose, using oxygen and raising BOD. Riparian planting and removing sludge reduce organic inputs, so they lower BOD.

questions.stem: A farmer sprays the same insecticide every season. After several years it no longer controls the pest. What is the best explanation?
options: The insects learned to avoid the sprayed crop and moved to another paddock
Each insect gradually became used to the poison after being exposed to it
The insecticide broke down in storage, so it was weaker in later seasons
Resistant individuals survived spraying and reproduced, so resistance spread
questions.explanation: Repeated use of one chemical selects for the few individuals with resistance alleles, which survive and pass them on until most of the population is resistant. Individuals do not acquire inherited resistance through exposure.

questions.stem: Which practice would best slow the development of herbicide resistance in weeds?
options: Rotating herbicide modes of action and using some non-chemical control
Spraying the same herbicide more often and at a higher dose every season
Spraying only half the paddock each year with the same single herbicide
Switching to a cheaper brand of herbicide that has the same mode of action
questions.explanation: Changing modes of action and using methods such as cultivation or crop competition means no single selection pressure acts repeatedly. A cheaper brand with the same mode of action applies the same selection pressure.

questions.stem: Nitrate fertiliser is applied to a sandy paddock just before heavy rain. Which impact is most likely?
options: Nitrate is converted to phosphate and makes the soil more fertile
Nitrate is leached through the soil and contaminates groundwater
Nitrate is locked onto sand grains and stays where it was applied
Nitrate evaporates from the soil surface and forms acid rain clouds
questions.explanation: Nitrate is highly soluble and is not held well by sandy soils, so water draining through the soil carries it down to groundwater. Runoff can also carry fertiliser to streams, causing eutrophication.

questions.stem: Nitrogen fertiliser is applied to a paddock that becomes waterlogged after rain. Measurements then show increased nitrous oxide release. Why?
options: Waterlogging speeds up nitrogen fixation by legumes, which releases N2O from roots
Water reacts directly with the fertiliser to form nitrous oxide without any microbes
Waterlogged soil is warmer, so the fertiliser boils off as nitrous oxide gas
Low oxygen in waterlogged soil favours anaerobic denitrification, releasing N2O
questions.explanation: In waterlogged soils, oxygen is scarce, so denitrifying bacteria use nitrate instead and release nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. Timing fertiliser to avoid wet conditions reduces these losses.

questions.stem: In livestock farming, methane is produced mainly by:
options: the photosynthesis of pasture grasses and clover
microbes in the digestive tracts of cattle or sheep
fertiliser reacting with rainwater in the paddock
the burning of diesel fuel in farm machinery
questions.explanation: Enteric bacteria and other microbes in a ruminant's gut ferment grass and release methane, which the animal belches out. Diesel combustion releases mainly carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Native vegetation is cleared from a catchment and replaced by shallow-rooted crops. Years later, salt appears on low-lying land. What caused this?
options: Fertiliser applied to the crops was made of salt, which built up in the topsoil
Less water was used by plants, so the water table rose and brought salt to the surface
The crops absorbed salt from the air and released it through their roots into the soil
Clearing exposed the soil to sea spray, which settled on the paddocks during storms
questions.explanation: Deep-rooted native plants use much of the rainfall; shallow-rooted crops use less, so more water recharges the groundwater, the water table rises and dissolved salts are carried to the surface. Irrigation that adds more water than plants use has the same effect.

questions.stem: How can poor irrigation practices lead to salinity?
options: Excess water raises the water table, bringing dissolved salts to the root zone
Irrigation water freezes in winter, which concentrates salt in the topsoil
Irrigation washes all salts out of the soil, so the river becomes fresher
Irrigation pipes leak salt into the soil from the materials they are made of
questions.explanation: Applying more water than crops use recharges the groundwater, the water table rises and salts move up into the root zone, where evaporation concentrates them. Salinity harms crops and can make land unproductive.

questions.stem: Seabed surveys beneath salmon pens find fewer species of bottom-dwelling animals than at control sites away from the farm. What is the most likely cause?
options: The pen nets release salt into the water, making it too saline for benthic animals
Uneaten feed and fish faeces accumulate, and their decomposition depletes oxygen
The pens shade the seabed, so the animals there have no food to photosynthesise
Farmed salmon dive to the seabed and eat all the benthic animals beneath the pens
questions.explanation: Organic waste from fish farms settles under the pens, and its breakdown by bacteria uses oxygen and can produce low-oxygen sediments that many benthic animals cannot tolerate. Benthic animals are mostly consumers, so shading is not the main cause.

questions.stem: Why can intensive finfish farming lower water quality in a sheltered harbour?
options: Farmed fish produce oxygen by respiration, making the water supersaturated with oxygen
Fish farms remove all nutrients from the water, so algae and seagrass cannot grow
Fish farms lower the water temperature, which slows the decomposition of organic matter
Fish waste adds nutrients and organic matter, increasing algal growth and oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Farmed fish release dissolved nitrogen and organic waste, which can fuel algal blooms and raise biological oxygen demand, especially where water exchange is slow. Fish consume oxygen by respiration; they do not produce it.

questions.stem: Salmon farmed in Tasmania are fed pellets that contain fishmeal and fish oil. Which environmental concern does this raise?
options: Feed pellets contain no protein, so farmed fish must be given extra antibiotics
Feed is made entirely from Tasmanian native plants, which removes their habitat
Feed sinks so quickly that farmed fish cannot eat it, so all feed is wasted
Feed depends on wild-caught small fish, adding pressure on wild fish stocks
questions.explanation: Fishmeal and fish oil are made from wild-caught baitfish such as small pelagic species, so aquaculture can rely on, and add pressure to, wild fisheries. Replacing some fishmeal with plant or insect protein is one way to reduce this.

questions.stem: A fishery targets one valuable species. Boats gain sonar fish-finders and larger nets. Within a decade the catch collapses. Which explanation best fits?
options: Better technology let fishers catch fish faster than they could be replaced
The new technology scared the fish away, so the population moved to another region
Sonar damaged the fish's hearing, so they could no longer reproduce in the area
Larger nets caught only juveniles, which are the only fish that do not reproduce
questions.explanation: Reliance on a single species combined with more efficient technology increases fishing effort, and when catches exceed the population's rate of replacement the stock is overfished. Catching juveniles does reduce future breeding, but larger nets do not catch only juveniles.

questions.stem: Overfishing occurs when:
options: more than one species of fish is caught by a boat on the same fishing trip
fish are caught using lines and hooks rather than nets or traps
fish are caught outside a country's waters by foreign fishing boats
fish are caught faster than the population can reproduce and replace them
questions.explanation: Overfishing means harvest exceeds the population's capacity to replace itself, so the stock declines. Where boats fish, and with what gear, does not by itself define overfishing.

questions.stem: Raw sewage overflows into an estuary after a storm. Which set of impacts is most likely?
options: Lower BOD, fewer bacteria and lower nutrient concentrations
Nutrient enrichment, disease-causing pathogens and high BOD
Acid rain, photochemical smog and higher tropospheric ozone
Higher salinity, less sediment and greater water clarity
questions.explanation: Sewage carries nitrogen and phosphorus that can cause eutrophication, pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, and organic matter that raises BOD. Beaches and shellfish areas are closed after such spills to protect health.

questions.stem: After a sewage spill, health authorities close shellfish harvesting in an estuary. Why are filter-feeding shellfish a particular risk?
options: They produce their own toxins whenever sewage enters the water they live in
They move upstream into the sewage and feed directly on the overflow pipes
They absorb salt from the sewage, which makes them unsafe for people to eat
They filter large volumes of water and concentrate pathogens in their tissues
questions.explanation: Oysters and mussels pump water through their gills to feed, trapping particles including bacteria and viruses, so they can make people ill if eaten. The same feeding method concentrates heavy metals.

questions.stem: Oysters and mussels in parts of the Derwent estuary have carried heavy metal levels well above food standards, with higher levels near a zinc smelter site. Why do such metals stay a problem long after discharges are reduced?
options: Metals are biodegradable, so they keep producing new toxins as bacteria break them down
Metals evaporate from the water each summer and fall back into the estuary as rain
Metals are produced by the shellfish themselves once they have been exposed to them
Metals are persistent, so they remain in sediments and continue to enter food chains
questions.explanation: Heavy metals are elements and do not break down, so legacy contamination stored in sediments keeps being taken up by organisms. That is why recovery of sediments and seafood after cleaner discharges can take many years.

questions.stem: An environmental flow is:
options: water allocated to a river to sustain its ecosystems and processes
the fastest speed at which a river can flow without eroding its banks
water pumped from a river to irrigate crops and supply nearby towns
the volume of rainwater that enters a dam from its catchment each year
questions.explanation: Environmental flows are the quantity, timing and quality of water kept in or released to a river to sustain its ecosystems. Water extracted for irrigation and towns is what competes with environmental flows.

questions.stem: Growing demand for irrigation water from a regulated river reduces flows below the dam. Which impact on the river ecosystem is most likely?
options: Wetlands dry out and fish lose the flow cues they need to breed
Floods become larger, so riverbank vegetation grows more quickly
Water quality improves, because less water carries fewer nutrients
Salinity falls, because extraction removes salt with the water
questions.explanation: Lower and more regular flows remove the floods that fill wetlands and trigger fish breeding and migration, harming ecosystem integrity. Low flows also concentrate pollutants and salt rather than improving quality.

questions.stem: Virtual water is:
options: the water reported in computer models of a catchment but not measured
the water used to produce a product, including water used along its supply chain
the water stored in clouds that has not yet fallen as rain over a catchment
the water lost from dams by evaporation before it can be used by anyone
questions.explanation: Virtual water, or embedded water, is the fresh water used to grow or make a good. Trading goods such as beef, cotton or rice therefore moves large volumes of water between regions.

questions.stem: A dry country imports most of its wheat from a wetter country instead of irrigating its own crops. In terms of virtual water, what is the main effect?
options: It saves its own scarce water by importing the water embedded in the wheat
It increases its own water use, because imported wheat needs extra washing
It has no effect on water use, because wheat contains very little water
It exports virtual water, because money flows out to pay for the wheat
questions.explanation: Growing wheat takes a large volume of water, so importing it moves that embedded water into the dry country without drawing on its own supply. The water in the grain itself is small; virtual water counts the water used to grow it.

questions.stem: Acid rain forms mainly when which gases from burning fossil fuels react with water in the atmosphere?
options: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
Carbon monoxide and methane gas
Ozone and chlorofluorocarbons
Oxygen and water vapour
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acids in cloud water. Carbon monoxide and methane are pollutants but are not the main causes of acid rain.

questions.stem: Photochemical smog forms over a city on a hot, sunny, still day. What is required for it to form?
options: Carbon dioxide from respiration reacting with water vapour in heavy rainfall
Chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerators reacting with ozone in the stratosphere
Nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds from vehicles reacting in sunlight
Sulfur dioxide from volcanoes reacting with sea salt in cold and foggy weather
questions.explanation: Sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, mostly from vehicle exhaust, forming ozone and other secondary pollutants. Still air lets them build up over the city.

questions.stem: Ozone in the stratosphere protects life, yet ozone in the troposphere is a pollutant. Which statement best explains this?
options: Ground-level ozone absorbs UV radiation, which heats the air near the ground to harmful levels
Stratospheric ozone is produced by vehicles, while tropospheric ozone is made only by plants
Stratospheric ozone absorbs UV radiation; ground-level ozone damages lungs and plant leaves
Stratospheric ozone is a different gas from tropospheric ozone, with a different formula
questions.explanation: Ozone (O3) high in the atmosphere filters harmful ultraviolet radiation, but near the ground it is a reactive oxidant that irritates airways and damages plant tissue and crops. It is the same molecule in both places; its location determines its effect.

questions.stem: Why does burning fossil fuels for energy contribute to climate change?
options: It releases sulfur dioxide, which is the main gas trapping heat near Earth
It produces water vapour that destroys the ozone layer above the poles
It releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years as CO2
It removes oxygen from the atmosphere, which lets more heat escape to space
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels contain carbon locked away from the carbon cycle for millions of years, and burning them adds carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, to the atmosphere faster than sinks remove it. Sulfur dioxide forms aerosols that tend to cool, not warm.
